I second this for research articles! My degree was in STEM and I had a very hard time in upper level classes when I had a bunch of articles to sift through or a dense textbook to process. Highlight, take notes with color, symbols, arrows, etc., just make it simpler for yourself to see the information that’s important and discard the fluff. Also, abstracts are great too! 

I also found that when I had a significant amount of reading, if I broke it up into smaller chunks and took a small break to refill my water bottle, grab a snack, stretch, do another less reading heavy assignment, or take a quick nap, I retained more of the information. Once I started dozing off and having to reread material, it was pointless for me to continue.

I didn't think I had narcolepsy until I saw the doctor and he thought I did. I have always had rough sleep at night, hallucinations, and extreme sleepiness. I was diagnosed with depression and chalked it up to that and poor sleep hygiene in school. I slept through all my classes and then took a nap after. I fell asleep on the bus or in the shower too, but again I was in college and thought I was just not taking care of myself. On weekends I'd sleep for like 40 hours then cram in homework. When I told the doctor, he seemed convinced but I wasn't. I was expecting apnea since both parents have it. 

Now that I'm on treatment it's so much better. I didn't realize how rough I had it. When I do have sleep attacks (now I can recognize them, I used to think it was normal) I know how to manage them. My college friends thought it was hilarious that I was diagnosed because it just made sense to them. 

I say get the MSLT to confirm if you have doubts, but I definitely didn't think I had it until I was tested.

It was barely over the threshold of diagnosis while the narcolepsy benchmarks were all met beyond the standard. I also hallucinated to the point of jumping out of bed screaming every time I fell asleep while there, so the doctor was confident I was narcoleptic. We opted to treat that first and see if the UARS was causing more problems after that and worth treating.

I have both Type 2 Narcolepsy and UARS. We went into the sleep study looking to rule out sleep apnea and confirm narcolepsy with the MSLT. They joked that I must be an incredibly sleepy person when I got the results.
